title: Deep Gaussian Processes on Directed Acyclic Graphs
claim: Different graph topologies induce distinct block-sparse structure in the inference matrix, determined by moralisation and chordal completion into cliques.
layout: 4 columns, graph above matrix, top-to-bottom, colour-coded cliques with outlined separators
description: Four columns labelled a–d, each pairing a small DAG (top) with its block sparsity matrix (bottom). Column a is a chain of three circles feeding a square. Column b has two parents, two middle nodes with crossing edges and two square leaves. Column c is a V-structure with a single collider fanning out to three squares. Column d is a three-layered zigzag DAG with four top nodes, three middle nodes and four squares. Dashed grey edges mark moralisation links and dotted black edges mark chordal fill-ins. Beneath each graph is a square grid labelled U1 to U4, U6 or U11. Its blocks are filled in colour-blind-friendly blue, orange, green, pink, yellow, grey and black, one colour per maximal clique, with bold black outlines on separator blocks. The matrices go from a simple banded shape to scattered, denser patterns as the graphs get more complex.
caption: DAGs discussed in Secs. 2, 3, and 4 (top row) and the corresponding block sparsity patterns of the structured precision matrix Λ (bottom row): chain DGP, disjoint routes (Thm. 2), V-structure with branching, and a three-layered DAG. Circles denote latent nodes and squares nodes with partial observations. With observations placed at the terminal nodes, each DAG is the ancestral graph of its observed nodes, so every inducing block contributes to Λ. Dashed grey edges denote moralisation (co-parents joined within each V-structure) and dotted black edges denote chordal fill-ins added to obtain the chordal completion H. Colours identify maximal cliques of H, with black outlines marking separator blocks.
abstract: Many real-world processes can be represented as compositions of functions along a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In causal modelling, these correspond to the underlying mechanisms; in engineering, to multiple fidelity levels; and in gene-regulatory networks, to transcription factors. These functions are partially observed across the DAG, with noisy and heterogeneously sampled measurements, posing significant challenges for reconstruction, uncertainty propagation, and inference. To tackle these challenges, we place priors over functions and naturally arrive at Deep Gaussian Processes over DAGs. We theoretically study their prior-collapse behaviour and the effect of graph topology and intermediate observations on the preservation of information. We obtain almost-sure lower bounds on the asymptotic frequency of depths at which the distinction between inputs is preserved, identify broad kernel classes for which these hold, and prove an observation by \citep{dunlop2018} on the role of input connections. We offer a structured variational approximation that retains graph dependencies, preserves compositional uncertainty, and captures the explaining-away behaviour of colliders. Finally, we empirically validate our theory and methodology at scale and under DAG misspecification. We then model a latent-collider DAG, a protein signalling network, and a multi-fidelity \mbox{heavy-ion} collision emulation task, attaining state-of-the-art performance while recovering low-fidelity contributions and yielding interpretability over the simulator hierarchy.
